title: Metano Prices in Abruzzo Have Surged 48% Since July — Even as Benzina and Gasolio Roll Over From Their September Peaks
dek: Abruzzo's daily fuel snapshot for November 19 shows gasoline and diesel cooling off from their autumn highs, while LPG and natural gas keep climbing — with methane up nearly half since tracking began.
executive_summary: As of November 19, 2026, self-service prices in Abruzzo stood at €1.965/L for Benzina, €2.234/L for Gasolio, €0.849/L for GPL, and €2.086/kg for Metano, across 608 of the region's 675 registered stations reporting that day. Benzina and GPL held flat to slightly lower versus the previous day, while Gasolio and Metano were essentially unchanged as well — a quiet day on the surface, with GPL running about 2.3% above the national self-service average and Metano running about 1.5% below it.

The real story is in the weekly data. Since Fuel Dashboard's tracking began on July 21, 2026, Benzina and Gasolio in Abruzzo have both rolled over from peaks reached in mid-to-late September — Benzina is down 8.8% and Gasolio down 5.6% from those highs — while GPL and Metano have shown no such turn, climbing in nearly every tracked week. Metano is the standout: its regional self-service average has risen 48.0% since late July, outpacing the 41.0% national increase over the same stretch, even though Abruzzo's methane pump price today still sits slightly below the Italian average.

fuel_sections.heading: Gasoline Extends Its Slide From the September Peak
paragraphs: Abruzzo's self-service Benzina price stood at €1.965/L on November 19, down €0.003 (-0.16%) from €1.968/L the day before. That puts the region fractionally above the national self-service average of €1.963/L — a gap of less than a tenth of a cent, effectively a tie.

Zooming out, Benzina in Abruzzo has fallen 8.8% from its tracked peak of €2.160/L in the week of September 21 (2026-W39), and is now 0.25% below where it started on July 20 (2026-W30). Nationally, the decline from the same September peak has been slightly steeper, and the full-period change is -0.43% — meaning Abruzzo's pump price has held up marginally better than the rest of the country even as both have round-tripped lower over four months.

fuel_sections.heading: Diesel Cools Off, But Abruzzo Still Outpaces the National Rise
paragraphs: Diesel self-service averaged €2.234/L in Abruzzo on November 19, down €0.001 (-0.06%) day over day, and €0.003 above the national self-service average of €2.231/L.

Like Benzina, Gasolio has pulled back from a September peak — €2.369/L in the week of September 21 — and sits 5.6% below that high. But over the full tracked period Abruzzo's diesel is still up 3.21% since July 20, outpacing the national full-period rise of 2.70%. In other words, Abruzzo's diesel climbed a bit further during the autumn run-up and has given back a bit less of it since.

fuel_sections.heading: LPG Keeps Climbing — and Abruzzo Now Pays a Premium
paragraphs: GPL self-service held steady at €0.849/L in Abruzzo on November 19, unchanged from the previous day, and running €0.019 (+2.34%) above the national self-service average of €0.830/L — the widest regional-to-national gap of any of the four fuels today.

Unlike Benzina and Gasolio, GPL in Abruzzo shows no peak-and-retreat pattern: it has risen in effectively every tracked week since July 20, up 6.59% over the full period to date. Nationally the rise has actually been sharper, at 9.18%, which means the national average has been catching up to Abruzzo's level rather than the other way around — explaining why the regional premium, while still real, has been narrowing from where it started the autumn.

fuel_sections.heading: Methane's Relentless Climb: Up Nearly Half Since July
paragraphs: Metano self-service in Abruzzo was €2.086/kg on November 19, unchanged day over day, and €0.031 (-1.46%) below the national self-service average of €2.117/kg — making it the one fuel today where Abruzzo residents are paying noticeably less than the Italian average.

That relative discount sits on top of the single most dramatic trend in the dataset: Metano in Abruzzo has risen 48.0% since the week of July 20, climbing in nearly every one of the 16 tracked weeks with no peak or pullback yet in sight. The national increase over the same stretch was 41.0% — seven points slower — meaning Abruzzo's methane price has been rising faster than the rest of the country even as it remains cheaper in absolute terms. If both trends continue, Abruzzo's methane discount to the national average could close within a matter of weeks.

network_section.heading: 608 of 675 Stations Reporting — In Line With the National Average
paragraphs: Abruzzo had 675 registered fuel stations as of November 19, 2026, of which 608 reported at least one price that day — a 90.1% reporting rate. That is almost identical to the national reporting rate of 90.4% (21,675 of 23,968 registered stations), so Abruzzo's data coverage today is representative rather than an outlier in either direction.

The registered count itself has crept up slightly since tracking began, from 665 stations on July 21 to 675 today — a gain of 10 stations, or about 1.5%, over four months. A reporting rate consistently in the high 80s to low 90s is typical for MIMIT's daily feed, since not every station submits a same-day price update; it reflects normal day-to-day reporting lag rather than stations exiting the market.

methodology_section.heading: Built to Run Itself, Every Day
paragraphs: This entire report — the price data behind it, the week-over-week trend analysis for all four fuels, the rotating choice of which of Italy's 20 regions to spotlight, and the prose you're reading right now — is produced automatically every day by an unattended pipeline built with Claude Code. A scheduled run pulls the latest MIMIT price and station-registry feeds (or a locally supplied same-day export when one is available), recomputes the region-of-day selection on a deterministic calendar rotation, regenerates the weekly aggregates behind every chart and figure in this report, and has an AI agent write up the day's findings directly from those numbers before publishing the dashboard update and this document.

That stands in contrast to the way a report like this is traditionally produced: a person manually downloading a CSV export each morning, pasting it into a spreadsheet, recalculating pivot tables and week-over-week formulas by hand, and writing a summary of what changed — a process that takes real time every single day and is easy to let slip. Here, the data refresh, the trend math, and the written analysis all happen without anyone opening a spreadsheet.

closing.heading: Explore Beyond Agip Eni
paragraphs: The live Fuel Dashboard opens by default on Agip Eni's brand-level view, but that's just the starting point — use the scope picker to switch to Region, Province, Municipality, or another Operator/Brand entirely and dig into whichever slice of Italy's fuel market you're curious about.

pull_quote: Metano in Abruzzo has climbed 48% since late July — seven points faster than the national rise — yet it's still the one fuel region residents are paying less for than the rest of Italy.
caption:
Today's Fuel Dashboard spotlight region is Abruzzo, and the standout story isn't the daily number — it's the trend underneath it. Since tracking began on July 21, Metano prices there have risen 48% while the national average rose 41%, even though Abruzzo methane still prices below the Italian average today. Meanwhile Benzina and Gasolio have both rolled over from their September peaks, down 8.8% and 5.6% respectively, while GPL and Metano just keep climbing with no turn in sight yet.

Fuel Dashboard is a live, self-updating site tracking Benzina, Gasolio, GPL and Metano prices across every Italian region, province, municipality, and fuel brand, refreshed daily straight from Italy's MIMIT price feed.

What I find most interesting about this project isn't the fuel data itself — it's that the entire pipeline, from pulling the daily feed to computing the weekly trends to writing up findings like the ones above, runs unattended every day, built with Claude Code. No spreadsheet, no manual pivot tables, no person re-writing the summary each morning. That's a real argument for building tools like this with AI coding agents instead of maintaining them by hand: once it's built, it just keeps running and keeps writing.
